validator: draft 1 passes: ok true, no problems, no soft problems, no warnings. whatAmILookingAt is 12006 characters, over the app's 12000 bound for that field, so trim it.
keep: The idea is named up front: the windings' resistance and leakage reactance drop a voltage under load, most when lagging, a leading load can lift the output, and the same impedance sets the fault current, so less sag comes with more fault current.

The picture is the brief's phasor drop: output arrow, I x R along the current and I x X a quarter-turn ahead, tip to tail onto a fixed 115 V circle, zoomed on the tip so every arrow is true to scale; a load slider, a power factor stepper from 0.5 lag to 0.5 lead (so 0.8 and 0.6 land exactly, which a 5-degree slider would miss), an impedance slider, and a fault-current bar that falls as the drops stretch.

One rule set computes every figure, and it carries lesson 5's transformer on: R% = 400 W / 10 kVA = 4%, Z% = 22.0 V / 440 V = 5%, so X% = 3% (lesson 5's 3-4-5 triangle). Exact drawing: 110.35 V and 4.0% at unity, 109.25 V and 5.0% at 0.8 lag, 113.26 V and 1.5% at 0.8 lead, 115.55 V and -0.5% at 0.5 lead. The rule R% cos phi + X% sin phi gives 4.0, 5.0, 1.4 and -0.6%, and the lesson says the drawing and rule differ by tenths. Fault current 86.96 x 100 / Z%: 1739 A at 5%, 3478 A at 2.5%, 2174 A at 4%.

At 0.8 lagging the load angle equals the windings' own angle (36.9 degrees), so the drop lines up with the output and the regulation is the whole Z%: the deepest sag, shown exactly, not just asserted.
The recall opener the brief sets (AC circuits lesson 6: 6 V at 0 degrees plus 8 V at 90 degrees) is screen 1, typed, with 'Still there.', and it pays off on screen 3's right-angled triangle.
Typed answers for every figure (screens 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12) with want, slips and hints; options only on screen 13, where choosing between two named transformers is the skill.

Misconceptions caught: regulation divided by the on-load voltage (screen 5, slip 4.2); regulation never negative (screens 7 and 12); R% and X% added straight or swapped (screen 9); higher impedance always better (screen 13, and the impedance slider's trade).

Footnotes only on the three rules he would look up: lead raises and lag lowers [^1], 20 times at 5% [^3], the trade [^2]. No source named in a sentence. Generators, AVRs and paralleling are left to the next course; three-phase groups to lesson 7.
fix: Skipped causal step, unity: 'the 3.45 V points across the output, so it costs little' does not say why. Say it only tilts the output: across, it costs as a square, 115 against 114.95 V, 0.05 V.

Skipped causal step, lagging: why the drop lines up at 0.8 lagging. Say the whole drop points 36.9 degrees ahead of the current, the windings' own angle set by 3.45 against 4.6, so a current lagging by 36.9 degrees brings it into line.

False claim, leading (screen 6 and explain): 'the output has to grow' with 113.26 V at 0.8 leading reads as if it passed 115 V. Give the step: the part of the drop along the output shrinks; at 0.6 leading the drop points straight across; past that it points back and the output must pass 115 V.
False absolute, screen 4: 'the deepest sag this transformer gives' ignores the 125% end of the load slider. Say 'at this load'.
False absolute, screen 2 and explain: 'Off load no current flows'. The core's small current still flows in the primary. Say there is no load current, so the windings drop almost nothing.
Qualifier dropped: the bold takeaway turns the quote's 'may provide better voltage regulation' into a certainty. Keep the hedge.

Practice: breaking capacity 'must exceed' the prospective fault current; the rule is 'at least'. The analogy's breaks says a shorter run 'cuts both its drop and its fault limit', which is muddled: a shorter run raises the fault current. Say the cable's impedance changes with the run, the transformer's is fixed when built.
Trim whatAmILookingAt under 12000 characters: shorten the picture paragraph.
shape: Idea in one line up front: yes.
